tldr: Emulating the "asynchronous muscles" of insects, this work reproduces the delayed stretch activation response using DC motors to autonomously adapt to wing mechanical resonance and collisions. It realizes the world's first flight-capable flapping-wing robot that can mitigate collisions without sensors or external control, achieving stable flight even in cluttered environments.
hero_caption: Overview of the flapping-wing mechanism emulating insect asynchronous muscles. The conventional method in the top row (synchronous actuation) drives wings using clock signals from nerves or microcontrollers. In contrast, this approach in the bottom row (asynchronous actuation) leverages self-excited oscillations that feed back wing motion directly. This enables instantaneous stopping upon collision, mechanical bilateral phase synchronization, and autonomous frequency adaptation under wing damage, all without controller intervention.
overview:
Insects with extraordinary flight capabilities, like flies and bees, do not actuate their wings with individual brain commands for every single stroke. Instead, they possess specialized "asynchronous muscles" that exhibit delayed stretch activation (dSA)—a property where stretching a muscle causes it to contract after a slight delay. Through the interaction between this property and thoracic elasticity, they generate high-frequency wingbeats via self-excited oscillations (limit cycles). In contrast, all previous flapping-wing robots have relied on "synchronous actuation," where a microcontroller sends fixed periodic waveforms to force the motors back and forth. However, synchronous actuation suffers from a major flaw: when wings strike obstacles or get damaged, they keep forcing their stroke until an external sensor detects the issue and a control system intervenes, often leading to structural failure.

In this study, the researchers engineered the world's first asynchronous flapping-wing flying robot (weighing 5 g) by replicating the principles of insect asynchronous muscles. Rather than adding heavy angle sensors, the robot estimates rotational velocity in real time directly from the back electromotive force (back-EMF) generated by the DC motors themselves, feeding back delayed stretch activation dynamics as motor torque to induce self-excited oscillations.

Experimental results demonstrated that this robot autonomously shifts its flapping frequency when wing inertia or resonance properties change, without any control adjustments. Furthermore, when striking an obstacle, it immediately cuts torque, reducing collision impact forces to less than one-third. By coupling the left and right wings with elastic springs, the robot also achieves passive bilateral phase synchronization. In cluttered environments filled with dense plants, it achieved far more stable flight than traditional synchronously driven robots. This work stands as a powerful demonstration of "embodied control," embedding intelligence directly into mechanical dynamics.
contributions: Replicated insect delayed stretch activation (dSA) using DC motors and back-EMF sensing, achieving the world's first autonomous lift-off and free flight driven by asynchronous self-excited actuation.

Demonstrated self-protective performance during wing collisions, instantly damping or halting wingbeats via purely actuator dynamics to reduce impact forces to less than one-third without external sensors or controller intervention.
Proved that upon partial wing damage, the system passively tracks the shift in mechanical resonance to automatically increase flapping frequency by up to 12.6%, compensating for lost lift.
Achieved stable bilateral wingbeat phase synchronization without electronic control, using a mechanical coupling inspired by the insect thorax that links both motors via crossed springs.

sections.heading: How do insects flap at ultra-high speeds without overthinking?
sections.summary: Many insects do not rely on neural pulses for every wingbeat; instead, their intrinsic delayed stretch activation autonomously drives wing oscillations. To overcome the control delays that conventional flapping robots face during environmental changes and collisions, this paper introduces asynchronous actuation to robotics for the first time.
sections.details:
Remarkable fliers such as flies, bees, and mosquitoes rely on two sets of muscles: large power muscles that drive the wing stroke, and small steering muscles that finely tune wing angles. Even more crucial is the operating regime of these power muscles. While some insects have "synchronous muscles" that contract once per neural impulse, most agile insects possess "asynchronous muscles." These feature delayed stretch activation (dSA)—contracting with a slight lag after being stretched—and resonate with the elastic thorax to generate self-excited oscillations without requiring neural timing signals.

Conversely, all previous flight-capable flapping-wing robots have relied strictly on "synchronous actuation," in which a flight controller dictates the time-history trajectory. While synchronous actuation provides direct control over wing kinematics—useful for complex aerial maneuvers—it is exceptionally vulnerable to environmental shifts and disturbances. For example, if wing resonance changes, continuous sensing is required to tune the frequency. When colliding with an obstacle, the delay required to detect contact and issue a halt command subjects the mechanism to severe, destructive loads.

If asynchronous actuation could be implemented in a robot, it would establish a limit cycle (a stable self-excited periodic orbit) governed by the wing's own state of motion. The actuator itself could then adapt to environmental shifts and react instantaneously to collisions without computing inputs. This study took on the challenge of realizing this bio-inspired strategy in physical robotic hardware.

sections.heading: Self-excited flapping without sensors: gliding through clutter
sections.summary: By reading velocity from DC motor back-EMF and feeding back delayed stretch activation, the 5 g robot achieves self-excited oscillations. Benchtop tests confirmed resonance tracking, impact force mitigation, and elastic bilateral synchronization. Finally, free-flight tests inside a cluttered obstacle cage demonstrated crash resilience far superior to synchronous actuation.
sections.details:
### Robot Design and Sensorless Velocity Estimation
The developed robot weighs 5 g with a 155 mm wingspan, driven by two independent miniature coreless DC motors (Pololu, 26:1 gear ratio, 1.25 g each). Torsion springs ($k_{\phi} = 12.9\ \mathrm{N\cdot mm/deg}$) are mounted in parallel at the wing base to replicate thoracic elasticity.

Realizing asynchronous actuation requires calculating delayed torque based on wing angular velocity $\dot{\phi}$, but additional sensors like encoders were too heavy to carry. The team focused on the back electromotive force (back-EMF) generated across the motor terminals. By sampling terminal voltage at 10 kHz during the high-impedance intervals of PWM pulses and capping the duty cycle at 0.7, they successfully estimated angular velocity in real time without adding extra sensors.

### Delayed Stretch Activation Dynamics and Autonomous Resonance Tracking
The dynamics of delayed stretch activation (dSA) are modeled as a second-order delayed transfer function with a rise rate $r_3$ and a damping ratio $\kappa$. Linear stability analysis yielded the critical gain $\mu$ needed for the system to undergo a Hopf bifurcation into self-excited oscillations, showing that stable flapping emerges when muscle (motor) response is faster than the mechanical timescale.

In experiments replacing wings with inertia beams to vary load inertia $I_{\text{load}}$ from $612$ to $854\ \mathrm{g\cdot mm^2}$, the flapping frequency autonomously dropped from 23 Hz to 20.5 Hz to track the shifting mechanical resonance, requiring no parameter tuning. This mimics the exact adaptive response observed in honeybees with wing damage.

### Impact Mitigation: Actuators That Relax on Their Own
When rigid obstacles were introduced during flapping, a stark contrast emerged between synchronous and asynchronous actuation. Because synchronous actuation continuously forces waveform trajectories, it kept pushing against the obstacle, exerting about 80% of its initial peak force on subsequent strikes. In contrast, under asynchronous actuation, halting the wing instantly dropped the velocity input to zero, causing motor torque to vanish immediately. During mid-stroke collisions, collision forces dropped to less than one-third of the synchronous values, cleanly stopping wing motion.

### Mechanical Elastic Coupling Between Wings
To synchronize the phase of both independent motors, the researchers replicated the elastic coupling of the fly thorax by connecting the left and right drive levers with two crossed springs. When both wings flap in phase, the springs remain slack and do not interfere; if they drift out of phase, the springs stretch to generate restoring torque. Experiments demonstrated that an initial phase offset of $\pi/3$ rapidly converged into symmetric, in-phase flapping. Even with asymmetric wing inertias, both sides harmonized to a common flapping frequency.

### Vertical and Free-Flight Tests Under Wing Damage and Obstacles
In vertical guide rail tests, clipping half of a wing rendered the synchronously driven robot unable to lift off. The asynchronously driven robot, however, autonomously increased its frequency by 12.6% to compensate for the lost lift and maintained flight. Furthermore, free-flight experiments with a drag plate were conducted inside a cluttered cage filled with plants and vertical poles. While the synchronously driven robot stalled and crashed upon hitting obstacles (resulting in short flight durations), the asynchronously driven robot absorbed impacts compliantly, maintained its attitude, and ascended all the way to the cage ceiling.

In contrast, asynchronous actuation (blue) cuts off its self-excited loop when the wing is halted, instantly shedding torque and reducing impact forces to less than one-third (B, C).

sections.heading: How embodied control outsmarts computation in micro aerial vehicles
sections.summary: This asynchronous approach bypasses the latency limitations of conventional sensor-processor feedback loops by handling instantaneous disturbance adaptation directly through physical dynamics. It offers an engineering perspective on why high-frequency insects evolved asynchronous muscles and presents a new design paradigm for resilient micro aerial robots.
sections.details:
Traditional robotics typically relies on detecting disturbances with high-precision sensors, calculating compensation commands via high-speed processors, and driving actuators accordingly. However, in miniature robots flapping tens to hundreds of times per second, the communication and computational delays of nervous systems or microcontrollers can be fatal. The self-excited actuation driven by delayed stretch activation (dSA) demonstrated here epitomizes "embodied control," embedding intelligence straight into the actuator's physical dynamics.

In particular, the collision behavior—where the robot avoids self-destruction and navigates obstacles simply by "doing nothing" (torque naturally disappears as velocity drops)—is an elegant solution that complex collision-detection algorithms or compliant mechanisms alone cannot easily match. Moreover, the ability to naturally increase frequency in response to lost wing surface area provides strong evolutionary rationale for why high-frequency insects like mosquitoes and bees abandoned nerve-pulse synchronization in favor of asynchronous muscles.

The authors highlight several directions for future research, including overlaying higher-level steering control (intentional behaviors like turning and trajectory tracking) atop this passive self-excited foundation. Furthermore, if delayed hysteresis characteristics like dSA can be embedded directly into artificial muscle materials, truly autonomous micro fliers that do not even require external motor driver circuitry could become a reality.

sections.heading: Engineering the 5g flier: experimental implementation
sections.summary: Using a real-time Simulink platform and high-precision DAQ hardware, the team built a 10 kHz back-EMF sampling and 2 kHz PWM torque update loop. The airframe was laser-machined from carbon/glass-fiber and PET laminates, with flapping kinematics tracked at 400 Hz using four infrared cameras.
sections.details:
### Implementing dSA with Simulink Real-Time
The control core utilized MATLAB/Simulink Real-Time paired with a DAQ board (NI PCIe-6343). Leveraging the characteristics of the motor driver (Pololu TB9051FTG), terminal voltage was sampled at 10 kHz. With a 15 V power supply, the back-EMF component was roughly 4 V; by thresholding out PWM pulses above 8 V and linearly interpolating the remaining back-EMF intervals, continuous rotational velocity $\dot{\phi}$ was reconstructed. The identified back-EMF constant was $K_e = 0.0157\ \mathrm{V/(rad/s)}$. This velocity fed into the second-order delayed transfer function (Eq. 4), and the resulting torque commands were converted to PWM duty cycles (clamped at a maximum of 0.7) and sent to the motor driver at 2 kHz.

### Microfabrication and Airframe Assembly
To survive intense high-frequency flapping, the wing flexure hinges were laser-micromachined from a five-layer composite laminate (two outer 0.03 mm glass fiber layers, a central 5 mil PET film, and two adhesive layers). The wings themselves were built as an ultra-lightweight three-layer structure using 0.01 mm glass fiber ribs and PET film. These components were bonded with 3D-printed connectors and metallic coil springs providing parallel elasticity, yielding an airframe with a total mass of just 5 g.

### Motion Capture Kinematics
Flight trajectories and wing kinematics were recorded using four OptiTrack PrimeX 13 cameras. Miniature retroreflective markers mounted on the body provided sub-millimeter 3D pose data at 400 Hz. This setup precisely validated the rapid amplitude attenuation during collisions and the ascending dynamics accompanied by yaw rotation during free flight.

takeaways: Physical testing demonstrated the extraordinary disturbance resilience of asynchronous actuation (delayed stretch activation), which adapts and halts naturally as a dynamical system rather than relying on active sense-and-react control.
Clever sampling of back electromotive force (back-EMF) provides a practical way to close sensorless velocity feedback loops on micro-robots under severe payload constraints.
Relying on mechanical coupling via crossed springs rather than electronic control achieves robust bilateral phase synchronization with zero computational overhead.
Embedding embodied intelligence directly into actuator dynamics offers a versatile design principle, extensible beyond flapping fliers to disturbance rejection in legged and underwater robots.
limitations: The current free-flight setup relies on a large passive aerodynamic drag plate for attitude stability, leaving the integration of active steering mechanisms (similar to steering muscles) for future work.
To sample back-EMF, the PWM duty cycle must be capped at 0.7, meaning the motors cannot be driven at 100% of their maximum power output.
Real-time processing (Simulink DAQ) and power delivery depend on thin tether wires, so fully untethered, autonomous flight with on-board batteries and computing has not yet been achieved.
